CausalEdge.description:
An edge in the labeled property graph representing a causal relationship. Carries all four annotation layers as properties:
  Layer 1: Claim strength and linguistic expression
  Layer 2: Philosophical account classification
  Layer 3: Sixteen causal features
  Layer 4: Evidential basis
Plus rendering metadata for each downstream target.

annotation_confidence.description: Annotator confidence in the overall annotation, 0.0-1.0.

annotation_notes.description: Free-text notes from the annotator about this edge.

annotation_timestamp.description: Date and time when the edge annotation was created.

annotator.description: Annotator identifier (human ORCID or model ID).

causal_language.description: How strong is the causal language used?

certainty_grade.description: GRADE-style certainty assessment for this individual causal claim. Controls downstream language in Rosetta Statement rendering.

comparator.description: What the effect described by this edge was assessed relative to. Answers "compared with what?" — a property of the causal inference, not an entity in the world, and therefore annotated here rather than as a control node. One entry per comparison arm, so designs with more than one contrast keep a separate description and comparator_node_id for each: a BACI design (e.g. Kramer et al. 1995) records one pre_treatment_baseline entry and one untreated_control or spatial_or_temporal_control entry. Use a single entry when the source reports one comparison.

context_dependence.description: Annotation of scope conditions or context dependence for the causal relationship.

contributing_sole.description: Whether the cause is presented as a sole cause or contributing cause.

determinism.description: Whether the causal relationship frames the underlying process as deterministic or indeterministic, or uses probability only to express epistemic uncertainty.

direction.description: Annotation of causal direction and evidence for direction.

ecosystem_context.description: The IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology Level 3 ecosystem functional group in which this causal relationship was observed, represented by an ELMO ecosystem type term. Use this edge-level field for the ecosystem setting of the causal claim.

evidential_basis.description: Annotation of the evidence type and evidence object supporting the claim.

fcm_weight.description: Numeric edge weight for Fuzzy Cognitive Map rendering. Range: -1.0 (strong negative) to +1.0 (strong positive). Stored at the state level: its sign is the predicate sign only, and the subject and object qualifiers are not applied, because they are part of each node's identity. A variable-level FCM multiplies this weight by the subject and object fcm_sign at render time (see the sign-composition rule in CausalPredicateEnum). Magnitude is derived from the predicate's fcm_default_weight, causal_language, and the strength annotation. Can be overridden by expert elicitation; record which in fcm_weight_source.

fcm_weight_source.description: How the FCM weight was determined.

id.description: Unique edge identifier.

mediation.description: Annotation of any mediating pathway between cause and effect.

moderation.description: Annotation of any moderator or effect modifier for the causal relationship.

necessity.description: Whether the cause is characterized as necessary for the effect.

negated.description: True if the source reports that the relationship does NOT hold — a null result. This is the canonical null-result encoding, and it is always paired with causal_language: no_relationship: negated is true if and only if causal_language is no_relationship. Leave the object node as it would be for a positive finding (the tested direction if stated, otherwise no qualifier); never encode a null result by giving the object node the qualifier "unchanged".

object.description: Node ID of the effect entity.

original_sentence.description: The full original sentence(s) from which this edge was extracted. Preserved for RAG retrieval and rendering validation.

philosophical_accounts.description: Which philosophical account(s) of causation does this claim invoke? A claim may invoke multiple accounts simultaneously.

proportionality.description: Whether the cause is characterized at a proportional level of specificity.

proximate_distal.description: Whether the cause is positioned as proximate, distal, or both.

reversibility.description: Whether removing the cause is characterized as reversing the effect.

source_document.description: Reference to an entry in CausalGraph.source_documents, by document_id.

specificity.description: Whether the causal relationship is characterized as specific to particular causes or effects.

stability.description: Whether the causal relationship is characterized as stable across contexts or conditions.

strength.description: Annotation of the reported strength or magnitude of the causal relationship.

subject.description: Node ID of the cause entity.

sufficiency.description: Whether the cause is characterized as sufficient for the effect.

temporal_extent.description: The temporal window over which this causal effect was observed. Distinct from the study period in source_document (when fieldwork was done): this captures the timescale of the causal relationship itself. E.g., "native recovery occurred within three growing seasons of invasive removal." Enables filtering by effect duration and analysis of whether effect sizes vary with observation window.

temporal_ordering.description: Whether temporal ordering between cause and effect is addressed.

token_or_type.description: Whether the claim concerns a specific causal instance or a general causal type.

CausalNode.description:
A node in the labeled property graph representing a causally active ecological entity — specifically, a state or change in state of an environmental variable or process. Merges ELMO's entity structure (Alamenciak et al. 2025) with CAMO's annotation requirements.
Key design principle: causation in ecology is represented between states or changes in state, not between things alone. A taxon does not cause anything by itself; the causally relevant annotation concerns the state or change of an attribute of a taxon. Therefore each node decomposes into:

  entity: what thing (taxon, chemical, abiotic factor, process)
  attribute: what measurable property (abundance, cover, rate)
  qualifier: whether or how it changed (present, increased, etc.)

The human-readable 'name' is the composed form: "Increased abundance of Canis lupus". The structured fields allow decomposed querying: "show me all claims involving Canis lupus" or "all claims about abundance changes" or "all claims where abundance decreased."
This pattern corresponds to ELMO's subject/object value + derivative qualifier + state/change qualifier structure.
For taxon-specific measurements a two-path model applies. Single-taxon measurements use entity_type: taxon, with the Wikidata QID in entity_term and the measured property in measured_attribute — the taxon node is both organism and measurement and participates directly in causal edges. Multi-taxon aggregates and ecological guilds ("native species", "shade-tolerant species") use entity_type: environmental_variable with one or more Wikidata QIDs or free-text guild names in applied_to. Causal edges are never used for taxon-to-measurement links; applied_to is a queryable annotation field only.

annotator.description: Annotator identifier (human ORCID or model ID).

applied_to.description:
The entity or entities that this node is directed at, acts upon, or whose scope the measurement spans. Covers two roles depending on node type:
(1) Scope role (environmental_variable): one or more taxa or ecological guilds whose measurements are aggregated or grouped — for example, "richness of liverworts, Sphagnum, and true mosses" (list the Wikidata QID for each group) or "abundance of native species" (free text "native species", tracked in NAO). Wikidata QIDs for higher-rank taxa enable downstream traversal to all taxon nodes sharing that QID without requiring a structural edge. Free-text values are accepted for functional groups and guilds with no Wikidata resolution (e.g., "native species", "shade-tolerant species", "invasive plants") and should be tracked in the project NAO list. Do not use on single-taxon nodes — use entity_type: taxon with the QID in entity_term instead.
(2) Target role (environmental_process and management_intervention): the specific entity that the process or intervention is directed at or acts upon. Use when the node's meaning is only complete with reference to a target — for example, "herbivory on Sphagnum" or "invasive species removal of Alliaria petiolata".
Accepts any entity type (taxon, community, habitat, etc.) using the same entity_type / entity_term decomposition as CausalNode.

embedding_text.description: Concatenated text used for generating the embedding vector. Typically: name + description + synonym list.

embedding_vector.description: Pre-computed embedding vector for RAG retrieval. Stored as serialized float array. Generated by the indexing pipeline, not by annotators.

entity_term.description: The core ecological entity as an ontology CURIE, or free text when no cached ontology term matches yet. This is the "what thing" — the taxon, chemical, abiotic factor, or process class, and is the authoritative ontology grounding for the node's entity. Corresponds to ELMO's subject_value / object_value slot. Examples: wd:Q18498 (Canis lupus), CHEBI:24279 (glucosinolate), ENVO:01000253 (grassland). Secondary ontology crosswalks, if needed, should be maintained outside article annotations in SSSOM files.

entity_type.description: High-level category of the ecological entity, for semantic disambiguation.

id.description: Unique node identifier. This field is populated automatically by the annotation tool; annotators do not need to fill it in. If entity_term is provided, Loom uses that CURIE; otherwise, Loom generates causal_mosaic:{slugified_name}_{4-char-hash}.

measured_attribute.description: The measurable attribute of the entity that participates in the causal relationship. Corresponds to ELMO's derivative_qualifier slot. Together with entity_term and state_or_change_qualifier, forms the full semantic content: "state or change qualifier of attribute of entity." This is the authoritative ontology grounding for the measured attribute. Use PATO terms for qualities (abundance, density, cover, height), GO terms for process rates, or free text if no ontology term exists.

name.description: Human-readable composed label for the node. Should express the full semantic content: "Increased wolf population abundance" or "Prescribed burning process" or "Elevated soil nitrogen." This is what appears in Rosetta Statements and graph visualizations.

parameter_options.description: Ways the state or change this node represents could be measured or supplied as a parameter, given as ids of ParameterOption entries in a ParameterOptionCatalog. A list of possibilities, independent of any source document: it does not record what a study measured. Used to bind nodes to data streams in digital twins and to choose observable variables when building causal models. Options apply to the variable, so nodes sharing a variable_key should carry the same options, filtered to those whose value_type suits the node's qualifier family.

source_spans.description: Text spans grounding this node in the source document.

state_or_change_qualifier.description: Qualifier indicating the state or change in the attribute, including cases where the attribute is present, absent, or unchanged. "unchanged" describes a reported stable state, not a null result; null results are encoded on the edge (see CausalEdge.negated). Corresponds to ELMO's direction_qualifier slot. Combined with entity_term and measured_attribute to produce the node's full meaning: e.g., entity=Canis lupus, attribute=abundance, qualifier=increased gives "increased abundance of Canis lupus."

variable_key.description: A calculated key for the causal node to assist  in BBN variable grouping.

CausalPredicateEnum.description:
Controlled predicate vocabulary for causal edges, grounded primarily in CAMO and cross-linked to Biolink / RO where possible. Each predicate carries a sign and transitivity property for FCM rendering.
FCM sign composition. The predicate's sign annotation and the nodes' fcm_sign annotations (StateOrChangeQualifierEnum) combine by one of two conventions, chosen once per rendering and never mixed:
(1) State level: FCM concepts are CAMO nodes as annotated ("decreased X" and "increased X" are different concepts). Edge sign = predicate sign. Node qualifiers are not applied; they are already part of each concept's identity. CausalEdge.fcm_weight is stored at this level.
(2) Variable level: nodes are first collapsed to variables (entity + measured_attribute, qualifier dropped). Edge sign = subject fcm_sign x predicate sign x object fcm_sign, with positive = +1 and negative = -1. A node with no qualifier counts as +1, as do the process_phase values occurred and ongoing (fcm_sign neutral), since the node is the variable's reference state. An edge with an unchanged node on either end has no variable-level sign and is left out.
Worked examples, variable level: "increased X prevents Y" = (+1)(-1)(+1) = negative; "decreased X causes Y" = (-1)(+1)(+1) = negative (the same finding, same sign); "decreased X causes decreased Y" = (-1)(+1)(-1) = positive; "removed X disrupts increased Y" = (-1)(-1)(+1) = positive. Applying node signs at the state level, or using only the object sign at the variable level, flips edges.
Only predicates whose sign is positive or negative carry an FCM sign. unspecified, variable, pathway, modifier and temporal predicates need an explicit fcm_weight or are left out of the FCM. Negated edges (null results, causal_language: no_relationship) produce no FCM arc.
CausalPredicateEnum.title: CausalPredicateEnum

CausalPredicateQualifiers.description: The predicate layer of a causal statement: the philosophical account invoked and the causal features of the asserted relation. A simple predicate (camo:prevents) plus these qualifiers, following the Biolink pattern, because an RDF predicate is a single IRI. Fields mirror CAMO CausalEdge Layers 2-3; 'direction' and 'strength' are renamed to avoid colliding with SEPIO's evidential direction and strength.

ComparatorAnnotation.description:
One comparison arm of a causal edge; an edge lists one per arm (see CausalEdge.comparator). Controls are recorded here rather than as nodes: nodes represent states and changes in state, whereas a control represents what a measurement was contrasted with. Modelling a control as a node forces either a hub node shared across unrelated studies or a per-study singleton that can never merge, and neither survives type-level synthesis.
Where the comparison arm is itself a management decision a practitioner could take — natural regeneration, cessation of grazing — annotate it as an ordinary management_intervention or environmental_process node and point comparator_node_id at it. An arm that exists only to be measured against gets no node.
A factor applied to every arm including the comparator explains no between-arm difference and is not a cause the study tests; it should not be annotated as a cause in that document's graph.

comparator_description.description: The comparison arm as the source names it, verbatim or near-verbatim. E.g. "natural (disturbed, unseeded)", "no treatment (control)".

comparator_node_id.description: Node ID of the comparison arm, where that arm is itself annotated as a node. Expected when comparator_type is passive_management_arm or alternative_treatment; normally empty otherwise.

comparator_type.description: The basis against which the effect was assessed.

status.description: Assertion status for the comparator annotation.

ComparatorTypeEnum.description: The basis against which the effect described by an edge was assessed — what the claim is relative to. Experimental controls are recorded here rather than as nodes. A control is not a state or change in state, so it fails the CausalNode test, but it is not neutral either: the same reported effect means different things measured against untreated plots, against undisturbed remnant, or against the same plots before treatment.

SourceDocument.description: Bibliographic metadata and study-level context for the source document. Supports RAG retrieval, evidence gap map construction, and spatiotemporal analysis of the evidence base. Spatial fields enable map-based evidence visualization and proximity-weighted retrieval. Temporal fields enable tracking of when evidence was collected and whether causal relationships vary over time.

sampling_effort_protocol.description: A description of, or reference to, the methods used to determine the reported sampling effort. Distinct from the survey method itself.

study_coordinates.description: Coordinate set or sets reported for the study. Use one entry per reported centroid or bounded study area. This supports multi-site studies without requiring site names that the source may not report. Coordinates enable map-based evidence gap maps, proximity-weighted retrieval ("show me evidence from sites near mine"), and spatial analysis of where causal relationships have been tested.

study_country.description: Country or countries where the study was conducted. Use country names or ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes where practical. If multiple countries are reported, separate them with semicolons.

study_design.description: Study design classification for EGM quality assessment.

study_duration_months.description: Duration of the study in months. Computed from start/end if both are provided, or entered directly if the paper reports duration without specific dates. Useful for filtering: "show me only studies with at least 24 months of monitoring."

study_period_end.description: End date of data collection. Same format as study_period_start.

study_period_start.description: Start date of data collection. Not the publication date — when the fieldwork or measurements actually began. ISO 8601 format. Can be year-only (2015), year-month (2015-06), or full date (2015-06-15). For paleontological or historical ecology studies, use negative years or descriptive text in study_temporal_note.

study_state_or_province.description: State, province, territory, or comparable administrative region where the study was conducted. If multiple regions are reported, separate them with semicolons.

study_temporal_note.description: Free-text note for temporal context that doesn't fit structured fields. E.g., "data collected over three growing seasons", "historical records from 1850-1950", "pollen core spanning 6,700 years."

TemporalExtent.description:
The temporal window over which a causal effect was observed or measured. Distinct from the study period (when was fieldwork done): this captures the timescale of the causal relationship itself. For example, a study conducted from 2015-2020 might report that invasive removal led to native recovery "within three growing seasons" — the study period is 5 years, but the temporal extent of the causal effect is 3 growing seasons (~18 months).
This is important for practitioners who need to know how long to wait for results, and for meta-analysts investigating whether effect sizes vary with observation duration.

duration_months.description: Duration of the observed causal effect in months. E.g., 36 for "within three years", 6 for "one growing season."

duration_text.description: Free-text description of the temporal extent as stated in the source. E.g., "within three growing seasons", "over a 20-year period", "immediately following treatment."

lag_months.description: Time lag between the cause and the onset of the effect, in months. E.g., if invasive removal happens in year 0 and native recovery begins in year 2, lag = 24. Null if the effect is immediate or lag is not reported.

observation_grain.description: The temporal grain at which the effect was measured. E.g., "daily", "monthly", "seasonal", "annual", "decadal." Affects interpretability — a relationship detected at annual grain may not hold at daily grain.

observation_seasons.description: Seasons during which the effect was observed, if seasonally restricted. E.g., ["spring", "summer"] for a growing-season study. Important for context-dependent effects that may not hold year-round.
